paragraphs: Scope: this page covers only O*NET 49-3042.00 (Mobile Heavy Equipment Mechanics, Except Engines) for career exploration. Actual equipment repairs, hydraulic and electrical work, lifting, and safety release must follow employer procedures and local regulations.

How to assess: use an entirely fictional equipment fault record to check whether you can describe troubleshooting steps, required tools and parts, hydraulic and electrical safety checks, result verification, and recordkeeping requirements, and retain verifiable records.

Who it suits: people willing to diagnose and repair mechanical, hydraulic, electrical, and pneumatic systems, verify work against manuals and manufacturer specifications, and stop equipment before escalating uncertainty.

Note: personality labels and interest codes cannot determine fit or qualifications. Exercises on this page do not authorize equipment repair, lifting, welding, or safety work and do not use real equipment or employer information.

Mobile heavy equipment mechanics (O*NET 49-3042.00) diagnose, adjust, repair, or overhaul mobile mechanical, hydraulic, and pneumatic equipment used in construction, logging, and mining, such as cranes, bulldozers, graders, and conveyors.

entries: Diagnosis and troubleshooting: operate and inspect equipment to identify defects, use computerized testing equipment and calibration devices to locate faults, and determine necessary repairs.

Disassembly, assembly, and assembly repairs: use lifting equipment and hand tools to disassemble and reassemble heavy equipment, and adjust, repair, or replace assemblies such as transmissions and track frames.

Component and structural repairs: inspect parts for wear or damage using micrometers and gauges, weld or braze broken components and structural parts, and fabricate parts from sheet metal when necessary.
Electrical and hydraulic systems: repair, rewire, and troubleshoot electrical systems, fit bearings as required, and adjust, repair, or overhaul hydraulic and pneumatic equipment.

Maintenance and inventory: clean, lubricate, and perform routine equipment and vehicle maintenance, schedule industrial equipment maintenance, and research, order, and maintain repair parts inventory.

Records and collaboration: maintain equipment repair records, test equipment and confirm compliance with manufacturer specifications, direct workers participating in assembly, disassembly, or cleaning, and hand over to relevant personnel.

paragraphs: Work context (O*NET Work Context survey): 100% of respondents wear common protective or safety equipment daily, 80% work indoors in conditions that are not environmentally controlled daily, 71% encounter hazardous equipment daily, and 62% are exposed daily to distracting or uncomfortable noise.

Pace and responsibility: 43% of respondents consider the consequences of decision errors extremely serious, 46% have high responsibility for others' health and safety, and 50% work more than 40 hours per week. Coordination with equipment operators, construction site personnel, and shop personnel is often required.

Capabilities and working methods: requires mechanical, hydraulic, and electrical knowledge, troubleshooting and judgment, the ability to read operating manuals, drawings, and technical diagrams, use maintenance management and diagnostic software, and consistently follow safety and repair recordkeeping requirements.

Main outputs: repaired and tested equipment and assemblies, fault diagnosis and repair records, component inspection and replacement lists, preventive maintenance plans, and performance verification against manufacturer specifications.

Key judgments concern accurate fault localization, repairs meeting manufacturer specifications, and whether equipment can safely return to service. Unsafe work or work beyond authorization requires stopping equipment and escalating first.

Adjacent relationships support career comparisons only. This occupation centers on mechanical, hydraulic, and pneumatic repairs of mobile heavy equipment; construction equipment operators focus on driving and operating construction machinery, surface mining excavating and loading machine and dragline operators on mine loading operations, electric motor and power tool repairers on motors and power tools, automotive service technicians on passenger vehicles, and bus and truck mechanics and diesel engine specialists on diesel-powered vehicles.
Compare item by item: who diagnoses and repairs equipment, who operates it, who is responsible for lifting and safety release, and who bears sign-off and handover responsibility.
Compare directions by repair objects, engineering outputs, safety responsibilities, and qualification requirements. Similar titles do not make duties and safety authorizations interchangeable.

Difference from construction equipment operators: they primarily drive and operate construction equipment for earthmoving and lifting; this occupation primarily diagnoses and repairs the equipment itself.

Adjacent fields include operating engineers and other construction equipment operators; excavating and loading machine and dragline operators, surface mining; electric motor and power tool repairers; automotive service technicians and mechanics; and bus and truck mechanics and diesel engine specialists.

AI task exposure for mobile heavy equipment mechanics does not equal job replacement. Technical information retrieval, test data organization, scheduling, and draft repair records may be assisted; people must retain final diagnosis, safety release, and sign-off responsibilities.

Potential assistance: repair manual and technical information retrieval, fault code and test data organization, preventive maintenance scheduling, and draft repair records. Adoption prerequisites: data permissions, reliable inputs, version control, and auditing. No automatic release: equipment safety release, on-site anomaly judgments, and final delivery.
Mobile heavy equipment mechanics must trace generated content back to original manuals, specifications, and actual equipment conditions; fluent text is not evidence of a correct diagnosis.
Verify sources and versions; spot-check edge cases; record human changes and escalations.
When using technology, mobile heavy equipment mechanics should first distinguish low-risk information organization from high-risk safety decisions, then apply different review intensities.

Low risk: manual retrieval, record organization, and reminders. Medium risk: analysis of candidate faults, requiring spot checks. High risk: decisions involving people, equipment, or safety release, requiring authorized approval.
Quality indicators for mobile heavy equipment mechanics should focus on repeat repairs, misdiagnoses, omissions, escalations, and outcomes, rather than processing speed alone.
Certificates, permits, employer appointments, and sign-off responsibilities for mobile heavy equipment mechanics do not automatically transfer through AI adoption.
Mainland China has no national occupational wage data with exactly the same scope as O*NET 49-3042.00. Manufacturing average wages can only serve as an industry proxy, not individual wages.
In 2025, average annual wages in manufacturing in mainland China's urban non-private units were 113,594 yuan/year (National Bureau of Statistics definition).
In 2025, average annual wages in manufacturing in mainland China's urban private units were 76,055 yuan/year. The two unit categories must not be mixed.
Actual compensation also depends on region, equipment type (construction, mining, or forestry machinery), site assignments and travel, shifts, and experience. Check actual contracts and local rules.
U.S. O*NET/BLS wages cannot be converted or extrapolated across jurisdictions into individual earnings in mainland China.

career_risk_cards.heading: Work pressures, risks, and boundaries for mobile heavy equipment mechanics

risks.mitigation: Release pressure, isolate, and confirm zero pressure according to procedures before working
risks.scenario: Disassembling and assembling hydraulic components without releasing pressure according to procedures
risks.title: High-pressure and stored energy release

risks.consequence: May cause serious injuries from crushing or falls
risks.mitigation: Qualified and authorized personnel verify safety according to specific equipment, manufacturer manuals, and organizational lifting and support procedures; no universal two-person permission rule is established
risks.scenario: Working beneath equipment with inadequate lifting supports or without locking them
risks.title: Lifting support instability

risks.consequence: May cause electric shock, short circuits, or battery fires
risks.mitigation: Disconnect and isolate power, verify absence of voltage, and use insulated tools before working
risks.scenario: Troubleshooting electrical systems without disconnecting power or isolating them
risks.title: Electrical and battery risks

risks.affected_roles: Personnel responsible for disassembling and assembling heavy components
risks.consequence: May cause falling components or personal injury
risks.mitigation: Use suitable lifting gear and follow a lifting plan
risks.scenario: Lifting and moving heavy components without a lifting plan
risks.title: Heavy component lifting

risks.affected_roles: Personnel responsible for repair records and handovers
risks.consequence: May cause repeat repairs, misjudgments, or faulty equipment entering service
risks.mitigation: Record using standard fields and have the responsible person confirm handover
risks.scenario: Incomplete repair and testing records or missing handovers
risks.title: Missing repair records and handovers

risks.consequence: May cause accidents, downtime, and compliance liability
risks.mitigation: Verify scope before the shift; stop equipment and escalate when it is exceeded
risks.scenario: Issuing safety releases or overhaul conclusions beyond qualifications or authorization
risks.title: Unauthorized return-to-service release
